title: Answer any market sizing question by building the estimate step by step from numbers you can defend
description: How many, how big, how much. The structure earns the points, not the final number.
hook: Being asked how many piano tuners work in Chicago can feel absurd, and a little unfair. But no one expects you to know the number. They want to see you build an estimate from things you do know, step by step, and check it makes sense. This guide shows you how, with a structure you can reuse for almost any sizing question.
body:
In this guide

  • Clarify what you are sizing
  • Guess first, then choose top-down or bottom-up
  • Sanity-check with the other method
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

Clarify what you are sizing

Units or value? One year or the total stock? Which country? Consumers, businesses, or both? Pin this down first: "home EV chargers installed in the UK per year, in units and dollars" is a very different question from "EV chargers in the UK".

Guess first, then choose top-down or bottom-up

Say an order of magnitude before you calculate: "My instinct is a few hundred thousand a year." It shows judgement and gives you something to check against.

  • Top-down starts from a big population and filters it: people → households → share with a driveway → share buying an EV.
  • Bottom-up builds from a unit: chargers one installer fits per week × number of installers.

Pick one, segment where it matters (urban vs rural, heavy vs light users), and use round numbers. Ask if there's a constraint on supply, such as fleet size, shelf space or installer capacity. Often the limiting factor is the real answer.

Sanity-check with the other method

If you have time, cross-check with the opposite approach or a known comparison. If top-down says 290,000 chargers and bottom-up says 30,000, one of your assumptions is wrong. Finding which is a great thing to say out loud.

See it in action: A clean top-down estimate

"New cars sold per year, about 1.9M; about a quarter fully electric, so ~475k. Around 60% have off-street parking → ~285k, and most of those, say 80%, install a charger → ~230k. Add first-time EV owners buying used, roughly 60k. So about 290k units a year; at ~$1,000 installed, about $290M. The limiting factor is off-street parking: only about 60% of new EV buyers can fit a home charger."

These are illustrative assumptions for practice, not real statistics.

What to remember

  • Clarify units, time period and geography first.
  • State a rough guess before calculating.
  • Segment sensibly, round numbers, sanity-check, name the limiting factor.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer. Getting some wrong is how it sticks.

1. What earns most of the points in a market sizing question?

  • Getting the exact real-world number
  • A clear, logical structure with stated assumptions
  • Using as many segments as possible
Show the answer

A clear, logical structure with stated assumptions. Interviewers know you can’t know the true number. They score your logic and judgement.

2. Why say a rough guess before calculating?

  • To save time
  • It shows judgement and gives you a sanity check
  • Interviewers require it
Show the answer

It shows judgement and gives you a sanity check. If your calculation lands far from your guess, you know to re-check an assumption.

Try it now

Estimate how many coffees are bought in London on a weekday. Say your guess first, then build it up.

Give yourself 2 minutes, out loud if you can. Speaking it, rather than thinking it, is what builds the skill.

Show a strong answer

Guess: a few million. Build: ~9M residents; about half drink coffee → 4.5M; ~1.5 cups each → ~6.75M cups; ~40% bought out of home → ~2.7M; add commuters and tourists, roughly +0.5M → about 3M bought coffees a day. (Illustrative assumptions for practice.)
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case. This guide is lesson 7 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress.
